senses.gloss:
dīkṣā
(‘observing a vow’)
------------------------------------------
Derived from the root ‘dīkṣ’ (‘to destroy इग्नोरन्चे by giving knowledge and wisdom’) the word दीक्षा has several meanings such as observing certain rules for a period of time, a rite to be performed at the beginning of a holy venture, like a Vedic sacrifice, the sacrament of उपनयन, receiving a मन्त्र (sacred formula) from a qualified गुरु and shaving the head as a part of a religious vow.
Dīkṣā is a must in all ritualistic acts.
Consecration of the sacrificer at the beginning of a सोमयाग is also called ‘dīkṣā’. It takes place after some preliminaries like an इष्टि and आहुति (offering a ladleful of ghee into the fire). The sacrificer has to wear a particular garment, a girdle of muñja grass and a piece of cloth as head-dress. He should also keep a दण्ड as staff. His wife should wear a योक्त्र (a belt of muñja grass). They are expected to follow certain rules during the period of the sacrifice.
Imparting a मन्त्र to a worthy disciple is called ‘dīkṣā’ in the tāntrik works. It is of several varieties. The गुरु can rouse the spiritual potential of the disciple by just a look or a touch. (See TANTRAS for details.)

dikpālakas
(‘protectors of the quarters’)
------------------------------------------
In the Hindu scheme of च्रेअतिओन्, as depicted in the पुराणस्, the eight quarters or directions (= dik) have been put under the protection of eight deities. They are known as ‘dikpālakas’ or ‘aṣṭadikpālakas’. They are:
Indra for pūrva or east
Yama for dakṣiṇa or south
Varuṇa for paścima or west
and कुबेर for uttara or north.
The intermediate directions are taken care of by:
Agni for south-east
Sūrya for south-west
Vāyu for north-west
and ईशान for north-east.
These deities are rarely worshipped. They are mostly represented on the central panel of the ceiling in the chief pavilion (mahāmaṇḍapa) of a temple.

Dīkṣaṇīyā
------------------------------------------
Vedic sacrifices (yajñās and yāgas) were very common in India during the ancient days. We find them mentioned not only in the Vedic and allied literature but also in the epics and the पुराणस्.
Somayāga is an important variety of such yāgas. Before a सोमयाग is started the दीक्षणीया, a minor rite of the इष्टि type (See IṢṬI for details.) has to be performed. The main part of it is the offering of पुरोडाश on eleven kapālas (pot-sherds) to अग्नि and विष्णु.
